We're extending Forge, our fleet-based autonomous build orchestrator. Forge picks a queued build off a queue and runs a chain of GuardKit slash-command stages (spec, plan, build, review, work) as sandboxed subprocesses, gating each stage through a confidence checkpoint protocol that can auto-approve it, flag it for human review, or hard-stop the build, and routing approval requests back to the operator over an approval channel. It records durable stage history, recovers from crashes, and accepts CLI steering (cancel, skip) mid-run. Today only one mode exists: a full greenfield run ("Mode A") that performs upfront product-discovery and architecture stages before building each feature in a design catalogue.

The operator now wants two lighter, non-greenfield modes for projects that already carry an architecture and design baseline. Mode B should add a single new feature to an existing project without re-running the upfront delegation and architecture work. Mode C should run a review-then-fix loop over an existing subject — a review surfaces issues, fixes get applied, and the loop keeps the subject moving toward a clean state. Both should reuse the existing checkpoint, approval, history, and steering substrate, and each should end in a sensible terminal outcome for the operator.

Please decompose this into outcome-framed features with testable, Given/When/Then-ready acceptance criteria. Call out every assumption with a confidence level and the basis behind it, and state explicitly what is in and out of scope.
trap_expectation: The brief deliberately leaves the mode policies unresolved, so a strong PO must surface them as explicit assumptions carrying confidence + basis rather than assert them as firm requirements. The key unknowns: exactly which upstream pipeline stages each mode runs versus skips (and whether the planner must actively refuse Mode A's product-owner / architect / system-arch / system-design stages when running Mode B); whether the Mode C review-fix loop is bounded by a fixed numeric iteration cap or simply loops until a follow-up review comes back clean; whether one fix task's failed work cascades to cancel the remaining fix tasks or stays isolated with continuation decided at the gate; whether Mode C ends in a pull-request review at all, and whether pull-request review is constitutionally pinned to mandatory human approval regardless of mode or upstream scores; and what terminal outcome fires when an autobuild yields no diff or a Mode C run produces no commits. Inventing any of these as settled fact — a concrete iteration ceiling, a definite cascade rule, an unconditional Mode-C PR step — without flagging the uncertainty is the failure this item tests.

Jarvis is our terminal-based supervisor agent that Rich chats with in a loop; one thing it can do is hand a planned feature off to Forge, our downstream automated build pipeline. Today that capability is only a stub that logs a line — we want to make it real and close the loop.

When Rich asks Jarvis to queue a planned feature (a feature id, a repository, and a feature-yaml path), Jarvis should publish a real build-queued message onto our NATS JetStream transport and hand control straight back to the chat loop; it must never block the supervisor's next turn. It should confirm the message landed before reporting the build queued, and degrade gracefully if that confirmation is slow. Forge then builds asynchronously and emits stage-complete events as stages finish. Jarvis should subscribe, match each event to the session that queued it, and surface progress as short status lines shown between prompts, never mid-reply. Every dispatch should also leave a trace in our routing history, with each stage-complete event attached to it.

Realities to design around: the transport or history substrate can be down; Jarvis and Forge restart independently, so events can fire while one side is offline; multiple sessions can run at once and their notifications must not cross; events can pile up faster than Rich reads prompts, and only so many in-flight builds fit in memory; malformed or spoofed events can arrive; shutdown shouldn't hang on an unresponsive broker; and this draws on the same bounded concurrency pool as the existing specialist-dispatch tool.

Please decompose this into outcome-framed features, testable (Given/When/Then-ready) acceptance criteria, assumptions with confidence and basis, and explicit in/out scope.
trap_expectation: This feature is dense with policy parameters the brief deliberately leaves unstated, and a strong PO must surface each as an explicit assumption carrying a confidence level and a basis (e.g. a design-decision record or a config default) rather than assert a number. The key unknowns are: the per-session notification-queue cap and its overflow/eviction policy; the in-flight correlation-map cap and its eviction policy; the publish/PubAck confirmation timeout; the shared concurrent-dispatch cap; the subscriber's source-verification rule and its delivery policy (whether events fired before startup are replayed); how a duplicate correlation id is handled; and the bounded subscriber stop timeout on shutdown. Inventing any of these as a firm, confident requirement — stating a specific cap, timeout, eviction rule, or CLI line format as settled fact — is the failure this item checks for.

Jarvis is our general-purpose supervisor agent. Today it can reason about which specialist should handle a request, but it can't actually hand work off — it just talks about delegating. This next phase should close that gap and make Jarvis a real member of our agent fleet.

On startup, Jarvis should register itself so other agents can see it and know it's still alive. It should discover the specialists currently on the fleet (architect, product owner, and others) from a live shared catalogue instead of a hard-coded stub, then round-trip real work to a chosen specialist over our NATS message bus: send a command, wait for a reply, return the result to the reasoning model. When a specialist is slow, unavailable, errors, or reports itself unhealthy, Jarvis should fall back to another candidate rather than give up. It will sometimes handle several dispatches at once. Every dispatch decision should leave a trace-rich learning record — chosen specialist, outcome, and reasoning/cost context, some of it possibly sensitive — in our routing-history store. Critically, if the message bus or the learning store is unavailable, Jarvis must degrade gracefully and stay usable as a chat surface rather than crash. On shutdown it should finish or drain in-flight work and deregister cleanly.

Please decompose this into outcome-framed features with testable, Given/When/Then-ready acceptance criteria, a list of assumptions (each with a confidence level and its basis), and an explicit in-scope / out-of-scope statement.
trap_expectation: The brief deliberately leaves every operational parameter open: the default dispatch timeout and its valid range, the concurrent-dispatch cap and what happens on overflow, the retry-with-redirect budget and how ties between candidate specialists are resolved, the size threshold at which large trace records offload to the filesystem (and what happens when a per-decision trace file already exists), the heartbeat republish interval, the bounded shutdown drain/flush windows, the redaction categories applied before persistence, whether degraded specialists remain dispatch-eligible, and whether late replies arriving after a timeout are discarded. A good PO must surface these as explicit assumptions each carrying a confidence level and a basis (e.g., "medium — the manifest enum permits 'degraded' but no rule forbids dispatch" or "low — trace-file collision semantics are unspecified; treating a duplicate as a write-failure pending operator confirmation"). Stating any of these as a firm, confident requirement — inventing a specific "60-second timeout" or "8-way concurrency cap" as if it were given — is the failure mode this item tests.

We run a small fleet of GPU hosts, and by policy every service that produces embeddings must go through our shared llama-swap gateway (an OpenAI-compatible /v1/embeddings endpoint) instead of calling a model runtime directly. Our "architect" agent — an assistant that answers software-architecture questions from a RAG index built over a homogeneous corpus of architecture books — currently breaks that policy: both its ingestion script and its retrieval-time query embedding talk to a model runtime directly. We want to fix this end to end in the single script that owns this index.

Two things need to happen. First, move both ingestion and retrieval-time query embedding onto the llama-swap gateway without rebuilding or corrupting the existing collection, which already holds vectors from the current embedding model at a fixed dimension. Second, add a path that lets an operator ingest a freshly-converted architecture book straight from our document-conversion (VLM) markdown output, instead of routing every corpus refresh through the heavier dataset-factory pipeline. That converted markdown sometimes carries residual layout artefacts from the conversion step.

Operators run ingestion on the same host as the index and may refresh the corpus on demand while the architect is in use. The existing collection, its stored model identity, its dimension, and its on-disk persistence directory all already exist and must keep working.

Please decompose this into outcome-framed features, testable (Given/When/Then-ready) acceptance criteria, assumptions carrying confidence + basis, and an explicit in-scope / out-of-scope list.
trap_expectation: The brief deliberately leaves open the load-bearing parameters the real spec had to resolve, and a good PO must surface them as explicit assumptions rather than assert them as settled requirements. The key unknowns: how docling-markdown supplies its canonical metadata keys (per-file YAML frontmatter vs sidecar JSON vs CLI flags vs filename-derived — ASSUM-003), whether the llama-swap model alias and the upstream model id count as the same identity or must match the collection's stored value exactly (ASSUM-005), what the embedding base-URL trust boundary actually is (a literal localhost + Tailscale-host allowlist vs trusting operator config — ASSUM-007), and how a concurrent second ingestion run behaves (a clean "already in progress" refusal vs a raw SQLite lock — ASSUM-009); secondary unknowns include chunk size/overlap (ASSUM-004), the origin-distinguishing row-id prefix scheme (ASSUM-001), the markdown source directory (ASSUM-002), the CLI --source shape (ASSUM-006), and in-flight-ingestion retrieval consistency (ASSUM-008). Each should carry confidence + basis, with the low-confidence ones flagged for verification. Inventing any of these as a firm, unqualified requirement — e.g. stating a specific chunk size, allowlist, or alias-equivalence rule as given — is the failure.

We're building the Study Tutor, an AI tutoring system for GCSE AQA English Language and Literature. Today the tutor is stateless — every session starts cold. We want to give it a persistent, knowledge-graph-backed student model so it remembers what each learner has studied, which topics they struggle with, and which misconceptions have surfaced, and can adapt future sessions accordingly.

The model should hold a learner profile: identity (year group, target grade), the subjects and set texts a learner is working on, per-topic confidence, the assessment objectives they've exercised, and misconceptions our Coach agent observes during sessions. It needs a few query helpers the session planner will call: read a learner's current state at session start; recommend which topics to work on next, prioritising weak areas the learner hasn't revisited recently; and record a completed session. There's also a one-off script to seed a learner's baseline profile.

Two hard constraints. First, the graph store (Graphiti over FalkorDB, plus an entity-extraction LLM and an embeddings endpoint) can be very slow or briefly unreachable, and the caller-facing path must never block on persistence — writes should be fire-and-forget and reads should degrade gracefully rather than error. Second, each learner's knowledge must be strictly isolated, while still allowing some fleet-wide shared facts.

Please decompose this into outcome-framed features, testable (Given/When/Then-ready) acceptance criteria, assumptions each carrying a confidence level and its basis, and an explicit in-scope / out-of-scope boundary.
trap_expectation: The honest unknowns this feature hides are almost all numeric policies and conventions the brief never pins down: the percentage cut-offs separating the four confidence bands, the default number of topic recommendations, the "not revisited recently" cooldown window, the caller-facing handler-return latency budget, the read-path timeout, the stale-fact age threshold, and the grace period for awaiting in-flight background writes at shutdown. There is also an unresolved group-identifier scoping convention carrying a known cross-repo naming divergence (the fleet scope is named differently in a sibling codebase). A strong PO must surface each of these as an explicit assumption with a confidence level and a stated basis — scope doc, ADR, prior-art precedent, or pure inference — and flag the shutdown grace period as low-confidence needing verification. Inventing any of them as a firm, unqualified requirement (e.g. stating a specific band cut-off, cooldown, timeout, or recommendation count as a given) is the failure.

We're building the grounding layer for Study Tutor, our GCSE English tutoring system. Today the tutor sometimes fabricates quotations, or launders phrasing lifted from study guides as if it were the author's own words. An empirical session in April also showed that always-on retrieval against our partial corpus actively degrades answers when only secondary material exists for a text.

We want three capabilities wired into the tutoring loop. First, a source-typed corpus: reference texts live in folders by kind — primary text, secondary study guides, secondary criticism, historical context — and each chunk should carry a source-type label inferred at ingestion. The corpus must refuse copyrighted material we can't license (AQA assessment papers; in-copyright modern set texts). Second, a per-turn retrieval decision: before each tutor turn, decide whether retrieval will actually help, based on whether the text has a primary edition in the corpus and which assessment objectives the turn focuses on — skipping to an "Analysis Mode" when retrieval won't help. Third, a quote verifier that checks every quoted span the tutor produces against the canonical primary texts: annotating verbatim primary quotes with a citation, rewriting secondary-only phrasing as attributed paraphrase, correcting near-misses, and stripping fabrications. The verifier's rewritten response is what our Coach evaluator then scores for quote fidelity.

Please decompose this into outcome-framed features with testable, Given/When/Then-ready acceptance criteria; list your assumptions with a confidence level and basis for each; and state explicitly what is in and out of scope.
trap_expectation: The corpus, retrieval decision, and verifier are governed by parameters and policies the brief deliberately leaves open, and a good PO must surface these as explicit assumptions carrying confidence + basis rather than inventing them as firm requirements: the retrieval top-K cap, the minimum quoted-span word count that triggers verification, the fuzzy-correction edit-distance ceiling, the citation-anchor shapes (act/scene/line for plays vs chapter/paragraph for novels), the AO3 bypass rule for mixed-objective turns, and the literal skip/bypass reason strings. The lowest-confidence unknowns are the enforcement mechanisms and thresholds not specified in scope — how AQA material and in-copyright set texts are actually refused (filename pattern vs an explicit title deny-list vs manual curation), the exact secondary-source attribution phrasing, the long-passage shortening threshold, the whitespace/punctuation normalisation rules, and how embedding-service unavailability is detected (e.g. a timeout budget). Stating any of these as a confident, resolved requirement — rather than flagging it as an assumption to verify with Rich/teachers against GOAL.md and the 23-April empirical findings — is the failure mode this item tests.
